overview: This record represents the early Chola world of the Kaveri valley around 200 to 300 CE, centuries before the medieval Imperial Cholas. Uraiyur and the port of Puhar were important centers. The imported outline is misleading: it includes Madurai and Karur, associated with neighboring Pandya and Chera powers, but omits the sampled coastal Puhar and Vanagiri locations. Their evidence below is historical context outside that outline. Neither the boundaries nor the century-long map interval should be read as the kingdom’s exact extent or lifetime.

periods.title: The early Chola atlas window
periods.summary: Royal poetry, inscribed pottery and excavated settlements illuminate a broader early-historic world; individual rulers remain difficult to date precisely.

sections.title: Kings and the evidence for their world

items.text: Early Tamil politics involved Chola, Chera and Pandya kings alongside smaller chiefs. The Cholas’ principal territory lay in the Kaveri region. Warfare, alliances and royal patronage connected these powers; the map should not turn them into one southern Indian empire.

Sangam poems preserve praise, conflict, love and descriptions of places. Their oral background and later compilation make their internal chronology difficult. They help us understand the early Chola world, but cannot be treated as dated eyewitness reports of every event.

Uraiyur’s early layers contained black-and-red pottery, other red and black wares, and dishes decorated with rouletted patterns. Excavators dated this broad Period I from roughly the first century BCE to the fourth century CE. These are everyday vessels from a long-lived settlement, not one king’s dinner service.

Floor levels with postholes were also found in Uraiyur’s early occupation. Such traces matter because timber-supported structures can vanish while holes and prepared ground survive. Archaeology can recover the footprint of ordinary building work even when no palace wall remains standing.

A brick installation at Uraiyur, interpreted as a dyeing vat, had square and rectangular chambers set diagonally opposite each other with paved floors. It belongs to the site’s early period. The structure gives physical substance to the town’s association with textiles: cloth production involved wet, messy work as well as skilled weaving.

Early Uraiyur yielded beads of colored glass, shell, terracotta and semiprecious stone. Bone points and needles were interpreted as weaving implements or possible writing tools. These small objects bring ornament and skilled handwork into view, although finished beads alone do not establish a bead factory.

sections.title: Water and a working port landscape

items.text: At Vanagiri near Puhar, beyond this map’s coastline, excavators found a substantial brick inlet sluice. Its widening curved outlet and projecting brick courses helped control flowing water and erosion. The report places this engineering in the early-historic port landscape, rather than proving that one famous king personally built it.

Kilayur’s port works near Puhar developed in stages: wooden poles preceded a brick platform and channel. The old timber phase predates the atlas century. This distinction matters: a port could inherit, rebuild and adapt its waterfront rather than spring into existence with a single ruler.

The lowest deposits at Vellayan Iruppu included an early-historic ring well and black-and-red pottery. Such finds document water infrastructure in the Puhar area. They do not establish a complete sewer network, universal clean drinking water or a particular medical system for the Chola population.

sections.title: Poetic glimpses of families and the shore

items.text: In Paṭṭiṉappālai’s extravagant picture of wealthy Puhar homes, women throw heavy earrings to chase hens away from drying food, obstructing children’s three-wheeled toy carts. It is praise poetry, not sensible poultry advice: even the imaginary traffic jams advertise the city’s riches.

The poem celebrates large kitchens with tiger-marked doors, imagining rice water running like a river while passing carts soil painted walls. Feeding people becomes a picture of abundance and generosity. This vivid scene should not be mistaken for a measured survey of street drainage.

Fishing households appear with small roofs, long fishing rods and nets drying in sandy front yards. Here the poem’s attention shifts from splendid goods to equipment that had to be tended between trips. A net on land was still part of the day’s work.

Another seaside scene describes people swimming in the ocean, rinsing in river water, playing with crabs and making sand dolls. The poem links washing, ritual and enjoyment. Its families are literary figures, but their beach-day pleasures are wonderfully recognizable.

A Uraiyur potsherd inscription contains antāṉaṉ, here copied in the catalogue’s scholarly Roman transcription. The authors interpret it, probably, as “Brahmana”, and associate the person with Mūlāṉpēdu. The inscriptions are dated broadly to the first three centuries CE. This is writing on excavated pottery, not a surviving schoolbook or a royal proclamation.

Tamil-Brahmi writing survives on pottery, coins, seals and rings as well as rock shelters across the wider Tamil region. Learning letters therefore had practical settings beyond monumental inscriptions. The evidence does not tell us that everyone could read, or that every Tamil inscription belonged to the Chola kingdom.

Early Chola political history becomes difficult to reconstruct after the Sangam horizon. Later accounts describe a Kalabhra interval, but the evidence for its rulers and sequence is limited. A precise fall in 300 CE would give the map’s convenient cutoff more certainty than the sources support.

By the middle of the sixth century, Pallavas, Pandyas and Chalukyas were important regional powers. That later political setting should remain separate from this early Chola snapshot. Tamil-speaking communities, agriculture, crafts and literary traditions outlasted changes in which court held power.

Puhar’s excavations also reveal later occupation and a Buddhist monastic phase. Those layers help explain the place’s continuing life, but they cannot all be used to furnish a scene set in 250 CE. A single archaeological town can contain many centuries of different households and institutions.

ending.text: The 300 CE endpoint is an atlas boundary, not a securely dated conquest or the disappearance of a people. Early Chola rule gave way within a changing regional order whose details remain unevenly documented. The later Imperial Chola kingdom has its own history and a separate card.
